h1: The 6 Best Printers for Cardstock of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Printers for Cardstock: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six printers for cardstock and card-making projects, from ink-tank models to compact inkjets and a mono laser, with caveats.
summary: The Epson EcoTank ET-2800 is the pick for frequent card makers watching ink cost. The Canon MegaTank G3270 is the compact tank alternative, and the Epson ET-4800 adds a feeder and Ethernet for office use. The Canon PIXMA TS6520 suits occasional projects with easier media control.
intro: Cardstock is where many home printers show their limits. Thicker stock can jam in a tray built for plain paper, and a printer that handles 20 lb copy paper happily may reject heavy cover weight altogether. The listing rarely warns you.

We reviewed six printers suited to card-making and ranked them on paper by ink cost model, paper path, controls and footprint. Important caveat: the listings here do not state a maximum cardstock weight, so check the maker's paper specs before buying for heavy stock.

products.name: Epson EcoTank ET-2800 Wireless Color All-in-One Supertank Printer
products.verdict: Cheap ink for people who print card after card.
products.description:
The ET-2800 is a cartridge-free EcoTank all-in-one that prints, scans and copies wirelessly, with bottled ink included. It sits in the $100-200 bucket.

The ET-2800 comes out on top as card projects eat ink, and refillable tanks cost far less per page than cartridges. The ET-4800 below adds a feeder and Ethernet, which most card makers do not need.

It suits frequent crafters and small card sellers. Check Epson's paper specs before feeding heavy stock.
products.skipIf: You print cards once a year.

products.name: Canon MegaTank G3270 All-in-One Wireless Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: A compact refillable-tank option for craft rooms.
products.description:
The G3270 uses a MegaTank refillable ink system, prints, scans and copies wirelessly, and is compact for a tank printer. It is in the $100-200 bucket.

The G3270 follows as it offers the same ink economics as the Epson, but the listing says less about paper handling, so there is less certainty about card stock.

It fits dedicated craft setups that want a small footprint.

products.name: Epson EcoTank ET-4800 Wireless All-in-One Supertank Printer
products.verdict: The tank printer for offices that also make cards.
products.description:
The ET-4800 adds an automatic document feeder, fax, Ethernet and wireless to the EcoTank design, and prints, scans and copies in color. It sits in the $100-200 bucket.

The ET-4800 sits third as the extras mean a bigger body, and a card maker pays for features the ET-2800 skips.

It suits a home office that mixes documents with card projects.
products.skipIf: You only want to print cards.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TS6520 Wireless Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: An OLED display makes setting media type easier.
products.description:
The TS6520 is a color inkjet with duplex printing, a 1.42-inch OLED display, a copier and scanner, and wireless printing. It is in the $50-100 bucket.

The TS6520 lands fourth as it uses ink cartridges, so card projects cost more per page than the tank printers above. The display helps you select media type for each job.

Choose it for occasional card projects.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TR4720 All-in-One Wireless Printer
products.verdict: A small office printer for light cards and scanning.
products.description:
The TR4720 is a color inkjet that scans stacks through its feeder, prints from phones and also handles faxes, in the $50-100 bucket.

The TR4720 holds fifth as its cartridge ink model costs more over time, and the listing is about office tasks, not heavy stock. It is the right trade for someone who scans more than they craft.

Use it for light cardstock plus document work.

products.name: Brother DCP-L2640DW Wireless Compact Monochrome Laser
products.verdict: Black-and-white inserts, but with warping risk on lighter stock.
products.description:
The DCP-L2640DW is a monochrome laser with automatic duplex, copy and scan, and wireless printing in a compact body. It sits in the $200-500 bucket.

The Brother laser closes the list as card makers mostly want color, and lasers heat the page, which can warp lighter stock. It does produce crisp text for inserts and booklets.

Pick it only for black-and-white card inserts.

whatMatters.detail: Printers list a maximum paper weight in pounds or grams per square meter. Heavy cover stock can jam or smear if you exceed it. Look for the maker's paper spec on the manufacturer page.
Cards use a lot of ink, so refillable tank printers cost far less per page. Cartridge printers are cheaper up front. Look for tank, MegaTank or EcoTank wording.
A straight, rear feed path handles thick stock better than a tight curved one. Many listings do not describe it. Check the manual for rear feed.
Lasers fuse toner with heat, which can curl or warp light cardstock, while inkjets spray ink. Check the engine type in the title.
A display lets you set the media type so the printer adjusts ink and speed. Look for OLED or LCD screen mentions.

howToChoose.intro: How often you print decides the ink model.

cards.label: Tank
cards.text: Lower running cost and bottled ink. Picks: Epson EcoTank ET-2800, ET-4800 and Canon MegaTank G3270.

cards.label: Cartridge
cards.text: Cheaper up front but costlier per page. Picks: Canon PIXMA TS6520 and TR4720.

howToChoose.note: Most card makers should default to a tank printer.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Low cost per page, a confirmed cardstock weight, and wireless printing.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Epson EcoTank ET-2800 has the lowest ink cost, but confirm the paper weight in Epson's specs.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You print daily or run an office. The Epson EcoTank ET-4800 gives you a feeder and Ethernet.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You print a few cards a month. The Canon PIXMA TS6520 will do.

faq.q: Can these printers handle heavy cardstock?
faq.a: The listings do not state a maximum weight, so confirm on the maker's page before buying.
Forcing heavy stock through a curved paper path, which causes jams.

faq.q: Is a tank printer worth it for cards?
faq.a: If you print often, yes. Ink is a major cost of card projects.

faq.q: How do I set up for cardstock?
faq.a: Select the paper type in the print dialog and feed one sheet at a time.
Let prints dry before stacking, especially on glossy stock.

faq.q: Is a laser OK for cards?
faq.a: The Brother is mono only and its heat may warp lighter stock, so it suits inserts.

finalTake: The Epson EcoTank ET-2800 is the best printer for regular card making because of its ink economics. The Canon MegaTank G3270 is the compact choice. Always verify cardstock weight with the manufacturer before buying.
